newsitem.title: INDIA: India says interest rate reduction could take time.
newsitem.headline: India says interest rate reduction could take time.

text.p: Indian Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia said on Thursday that a reduction in interest rates to world levels sought by industry could take three to four years because of fiscal constraints.

Ahluwalia told a business seminar that in order to bring down interest rates, the government needed to control inflation and also cut fiscal deficit by reducing government borrowings, a process that could take time.
"We have a long way to go, hopefully three to four years...meanwhile, we will continue to have interest rates higher than world levels," he said.
Arun Bharat Ram, one of India's leading industrialists, told Ahluwalia that firms had to borrow at interest rates as high as 19 to 20 percent.
"Yes, it is true that interest rates are higher (than world levels)," Ahluwalia said. "But the trouble is it is a long process (to reduce interest rates) and there is no quick way to do that."

The government did not want to apply a credit squeeze to control inflation and instead wanted to control fiscal deficit and government borrowings, which would release a huge amount of funds into the monetary system, he said.

India's fiscal deficit is aimed to be controlled to 4.5 percent in 1997/98 (April-March) from an expected 5.0 percent in 1996/97. In 1990-91, when India started an economic reform programme, it was more than 8.0 percent.
Inflation, which was around 17 percent when India launched economic reforms, is currently just below eight percent.

Ahluwalia said Indian banks had become wary of lending to borrowers without verifying their track records following financial sector reforms that initiated steps to ensure prudent lending with appropriate capital adequacy ratios.
"I have been told nobody who has a top-class credit record is not getting credit," he said.
